name: EAGLE

claims.claim_text: The free edition is limited by board geometry rather than by output quality: two layers, a single schematic sheet and a bounded board size, with no watermark or crippling of the files it produces.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's limited in size one one schematic sheet
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Loopback

claims.claim_text: That size limit is dimensional rather than by area, so a long thin board covering less total area than the permitted rectangle still exceeds the free licence and forces the top-tier purchase.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I want to make one long, thin, tiny board, which is less surface area than one big 100 millimeters by 80 millimeters
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: The licence tiers step steeply: exceeding two layers or the free board size costs several hundred dollars, and the unrestricted edition ran to a thousand dollars or more, which is the arithmetic that decides whether a hobby project can grow inside the tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: if my board's bigger than, what, 80 by 100 millimeters, which isn't that big, right? Or more than two layers. I've got to spend 500 bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: Commercial use requires a paid licence at any scale, which is what stops a design made in the free edition from being straightforwardly reproducible by anyone who receives the files.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't do any commercial stuff at all without paying the license
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: A workable test of whether a published design is genuinely open is whether one other person anywhere can build it: a design whose files can only be opened by buying an expensive licence fails that test regardless of what its licence says.
claims.quote_verbatim: can one person in the world build what you built?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: The free edition is what made the tool the default in open hardware: without it the position would not have been reached, and the community libraries that grew on top of it are what kept designs there afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: The free version is what made them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Science, Not Silence

claims.claim_text: The vendor's own position was that the tool did not compete with high-end packages and deliberately served the low end, which is consistent with what practitioners found when routing large ball-grid-array parts that need many layers.
claims.quote_verbatim: Eagle can't compete with the higher end packages
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: CAD programs, Systems Design and Renewable Energy

claims.claim_text: Dense boards carrying two or three ball-grid-array packages have been built in it, so the constraint is effort rather than capability; four-layer work is possible but is the hard way to do it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've used Eagle to try to do four layer stuff and it, I mean, it, it works, it works all right, but it's kind of the hard way to do it
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: The tool changed remarkably little across roughly fifteen years: a licence holder from 2010 found the current release essentially the same product, with awkward operations such as changing annular ring sizes on a per-component basis still unaddressed.
claims.quote_verbatim: changing pad, annular ring sizes on, like, a per-component basis is still a nightmare
claims.episode_title: A Keyzermas Story

claims.claim_text: The upgrade case is made on time rather than features: a team doing four-layer flex work, bill-of-materials management and scripted output generation found the hours lost fighting the tool exceeded the price difference, switching at a point where the cheaper package cost about eight hundred dollars against roughly twenty-two hundred a year for the professional one.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm spending a lot of time fighting Eagle
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: Bundled footprints are the tool's weakest component: the supplied library parts are oversized and unreliable enough that experienced users generate essentially all of their own footprints by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: the footprints that come with Eagle are almost useless
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: DJ and Jazzy Jeff

claims.claim_text: The standards body's recommended land patterns follow a formula based on the component's geometry together with the statistical variation of placement accuracy, which can be reduced to a spreadsheet for chip resistors and capacitors; anything more complex than that sends the designer back to a generator or the specification itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's based on the geometry of the components as well as like statistical variations in placing accuracy
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: DJ and Jazzy Jeff

claims.claim_text: A defective footprint in a widely copied library propagates into assembly defects: one 0402 land pattern from the standard library produces tombstoning and head-in-pillow failures at a contract assembler often enough that the assembler wrote and circulated a corrected replacement.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is an 0402 footprint in the Eagle library that haunts me
claims.speaker: Chris Denney
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: The library model binds a package to each device variant, so choosing the part in the schematic already fixes its footprint, where other tools carry only the symbol into the schematic and assign the footprint at layout; the same librarian work happens either way, but at different points in the flow.
claims.quote_verbatim: in Eagle, it's actually linked together
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Where a vendor maintains a public library, accepting user-contributed parts by pull request is what keeps coverage current for boards old enough that their components were never added.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can have our customers design those parts and then, you know, just issue a pull request
claims.speaker: Tony Kloppenstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Design rule checking is not enforced as part of the flow, so a board can be sent to fabrication without ever having been checked, which is a class of error the tool does not prevent.
claims.quote_verbatim: This is what happens when you use Eagle and the DRC isn't built in
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Re-scoping the problem

claims.claim_text: The move to an open XML file format was the change that made the design data portable, because other tools could then read it directly rather than through reverse-engineered importers.
claims.quote_verbatim: Eagle now uses the open source XML format
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: That portability is what allowed competing tools to accept the files natively, and by the time one open tool reached its fifth version the import was solid enough to bring in whole projects including libraries.
claims.quote_verbatim: Eagle files are now portable for a lot of these things
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: In practice the conversion still fails in specific ways: an import of a published design produced errors and left power planes unconnected, and users have written their own import scripts to work around gaps in the supplied one.
claims.quote_verbatim: the power planes aren't connected
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Living Through Chipageddon

claims.claim_text: Nobody should expect a perfect importer; if the conversion work does not appear in redrawing, it appears in verifying that what came across is right.
claims.quote_verbatim: Nobody ever expects a perfect importer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Just Terrestrial and Space Things

claims.claim_text: Import damage persists beyond the conversion, because the library comes across with it: a component that arrives carrying twelve layers it does not need puts those layers on every future board that uses it.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have like 12 extra layers that you don't need on every component
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Rebuilding Projects with Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Older designs can become unopenable as versions move on, which is the archival argument for keeping the tool that produced a design alongside the design itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: I designed some things in Eagle years ago and now I can't open them
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Generating library parts in a neutral format and exporting per tool works for ordinary symbols and pads but breaks on features the tools represent differently; slotted holes are the hard case, and in this tool they must be drawn on the milling layer because there is no slotted-hole primitive at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: we need to use the milling, you know, the milling layer because there isn't like an actual slotted hole element
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: One component-library service reported its downloads running at roughly thirty percent for the leading professional tool, about twenty-five percent for this one, and around fifteen percent each for three others, which is a proxy for what designers actually have installed.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium is probably like 30%. Eagle is probably like 25%
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: A low-volume board house watching its own order mix saw the balance invert over a few years: almost entirely this tool at the outset with a little of the open alternative, then the open tool rising to around three quarters, and later a broader mix as professional firms began sending boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was almost all Eagle with a little bit of
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Both this tool and the leading professional package carry high unlicensed use, with the professional package effectively the standard in one large market almost entirely without payment.
claims.quote_verbatim: Eagle and Altium seem to both have both high piracy rates
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Inside large companies with only a handful of floating seats of the official tool, engineers use the cheap package for small adapter boards, because going through the sanctioned channel can take weeks just to have a footprint defined.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's some guy who is using like Eagle to do his little board
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Keyzermas Vacation

claims.claim_text: Autorouting is dominated by setup rather than by the run: roughly nine tenths of the effort is configuring constraints and one tenth is pressing the button and tidying afterwards, and there is a case that a low-end package should spend its development effort on the layout editor instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: an auto router is 90% set up and 10% is where you hit the button
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Autorouter, Datasheets & Obscure Chips - Cloddish Collegiate Conversations

claims.claim_text: An external open router exists that links into this tool and several others as their autorouter, so the capability does not have to be built into each package.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a web-based router. It's an open source, you know, router
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: The interface was later reorganised from grouping commands by kind to ordering them by workflow: set up layers, define the board outline, place components, route them, pour polygons, then rip up and rework, arranged left to right in the order most users proceed.
claims.quote_verbatim: how do I set up my layers, define a board outline, place components, route them together
claims.speaker: Matt Berggren
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Berggren

claims.claim_text: A single-connection routing command was added deliberately as groundwork rather than as a general autorouter: once one connection can be routed and length-tuned on command, a rip-up-and-reroute-device command becomes possible, and from there a mechanical engineer moving a connector can have the affected connections rerouted automatically.
claims.quote_verbatim: one click, one kill route something
claims.speaker: Matt Berggren
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Berggren

claims.claim_text: Electrical and mechanical integration was built by inserting the board into the mechanical model's timeline as a sketch that is then extruded into the board shape, rather than by exchanging static geometry through a neutral format; the difference matters because downstream mechanical operations recalculate when the board changes.
claims.quote_verbatim: we insert the PCB into the timeline
claims.speaker: Matt Berggren
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Berggren

claims.claim_text: Reusable schematic blocks were added in response to the observation that engineers solve the same small problems repeatedly in isolated environments with no way to pass the solutions between them.
claims.quote_verbatim: Matt's really big on like design reuse and he pulled that into Eagle
claims.episode_title: Grad School Time Capsule with Joshua and Zach

claims.claim_text: Ownership moved twice: the distributor that had bought the original German company sold it on for a reported figure in the region of twenty million dollars, after which it passed to a mechanical CAD vendor.
claims.quote_verbatim: Rumor has it, maybe about in the $20 million range
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Catalyzing Change Agents

claims.claim_text: The end state was announced years later: the standalone product was discontinued in favour of the electronics module inside the acquirer's mechanical CAD package, which descends from it, with disagreement among practitioners about how much of the original code carried over as against a rewrite.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're investing all their time in a fusion 360 or fusion electronics
claims.episode_title: Discovering Cursed Connectors

claims.claim_text: A mechanical CAD vendor acquiring an electronics tool has no interest in serving a hobby market, which is the structural reason such a product gets folded into a larger suite rather than kept as a cheap standalone.
claims.quote_verbatim: Autodesk don't want a hobby solution
claims.episode_title: Discovering Cursed Connectors

claims.claim_text: The move to online subscription is what caused a working shop to leave: a competitor cut its price sharply at the same moment specifically to capture users displaced by that licensing change, so the switch was driven by a competitor's terms rather than by a feature comparison.
claims.quote_verbatim: when Eagle decided they were going to change their, their, their, you know, their thing to an online subscription base
claims.speaker: Charles Alexanian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Charles Alexanian

claims.claim_text: Withdrawal of the perpetual licence was the specific trigger for one consultancy to move its new work elsewhere while deliberately retaining the old licence to support legacy designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: When they went away from the perpetual license, I was like, ah, it's not going to work for me
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Rebuilding Projects with Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The corresponding practice is to freeze the old tool with the old work: keep the perpetual licence and the designs it produced together as an archive, and send only new projects to the replacement tool, rather than attempting to convert a back catalogue.
claims.quote_verbatim: lock that with your old designs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Science, Not Silence

claims.claim_text: Changing design tools is not a decision that can be made on a whim; it usually requires an external trigger such as leaving a job and the licence behind, because the relearning cost falls entirely on the designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you have some kind of change agent in your life
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Catalyzing Change Agents

claims.claim_text: The cost of switching is a deliberate period of reduced output: an experienced user opening the alternative finds nothing where expected, and the change only happens if the designer accepts that performance hit knowingly.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to take the performance hit for a while to overcome that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Timing is Everything

claims.claim_text: The opposing position is that a free base version from any vendor is adequate to get a board made, and that time spent troubleshooting a tool's own defects is time not spent on the board; the practitioner holding it bought a professional licence at twenty-five hundred dollars and justified it against revenue from books whose boards it produced.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want to deal with your bugs that you put
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Starting a derivative board from a published design's own files rather than from its documentation removes a class of error: taking the header positions and outline directly from the source design means the connector geometry cannot be transcribed wrongly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a lot harder to be wrong when you're starting from the actual design files
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Kridner and Robert Nelson

claims.claim_text: Equipment vendors integrate with whichever tool holds the hobby market: a desktop milling machine shipped software that went directly from this tool's files to board routing, because that was where its customers' designs already were.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have really fancy software to go straight from Eagle to board routing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The 2014 Maker Faire Show - Traveling Technology Trangam

claims.claim_text: Assembly services can extract most of what they need from the native files of this and the other common tools, but paste aperture centres for a dispenser are a separate output that the design files do not directly provide.
claims.quote_verbatim: we get most of the data we can get from Eagle, KiCad, and DipTrace
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: A mid-priced competitor was positioned at three to four thousand dollars, which sat between the free tier and the professional tools and attracted neither, and was later cut to nine hundred and ninety-five dollars with a hundred and twenty-five dollar annual maintenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was the dead zone. It was the no man's land of CAD pricing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Catalyzing Change Agents

claims.claim_text: A rival free offering took the opposite approach to limiting its free tier, imposing no size or layer restrictions at all but requiring that projects be published, which trades a geometric constraint for a disclosure one.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are no limits. But the catch was, is that you had to make everything public
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: Free tools without size limits appeared and did not displace the incumbent, because entrenchment in an existing user base and its libraries outweighs a better free tier for people who already have designs in a format.
claims.quote_verbatim: The Eagle's too entrenched
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

attribution_notes: ep 471: labels flagged unreliable, but the passages are self-consistently the guest describing product decisions he made for the tool's interface and its mechanical integration; content-attributed to Matt Berggren.

ep 523, 531, 537, 611, 636: labels flagged unreliable; claims are attributed by content (a long-time licence holder, a component-library service, a consultancy that switched tools, a design-reuse advocate and an end-of-life announcement) and carry no name unless the identity is itself the content.
Three passages carried no episode number and were dropped before extraction.
Host preference material about which tool anyone likes, and the campaign to make the tool free, was discarded; licence mechanics and their design consequences were kept.
